AMENDMENT to this task's scope and cost, from verifying the proposed mechanism against #1773's completed full-dictionary run. Two changes: the mechanism is narrower than the body states, and the blast radius is larger.

## 1. MECHANISM — narrower and sharper than "markdown fencing breaks the parser"

Verified in source. `parse_judge_json` tries `json.loads(text)`, then `start = text.index("{")` + `raw_decode(text, start)` — the FIRST brace. A CLEANLY fenced response therefore parses FINE, because the first `{` is the real object. Measured on #1773's axes probe: 35 of 60 responses were fenced and 60 of 60 parsed.

The failing subset is specifically responses where a brace PRECEDES the object — a preamble or reasoning prose containing `{` — which sends `raw_decode` to the wrong offset. That reconciles the rates the original body could not: ~58% fencing but only ~2% failures, and why a fence-strip recovers 29/40 (the strip skips the offending preamble as a side effect).

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX: target BRACE-CANDIDATE ITERATION, not fencing per se. Iterate candidate `{` offsets and `raw_decode` at each, returning the first success (or the largest successful object); a fence-strip alone is a partial remedy that happens to work by discarding the preamble. Drop-never-coerce stays intact.

## 2. PROPAGATED GAP — the describe drop silently degraded 2% of the AXIS labels

This was not in the original filing and is the more important half.

All five axes consume the description (`AXIS_SEES` in `scripts/issue1773_common.py:175-181` lists `DESC` for abstraction, speaker_property, content_type, functional_role, interpretable). The renderer at `issue1773_common.py:432` is:

    if "DESC" in sees and description:
        parts.append(f"### Feature description\n{description}")

A MISSING description is therefore SILENTLY OMITTED — no crash, no warning, no marker, and no field in the output schema recording it (`axis_labels.jsonl` carries axis / feat_id / label / labels_surviving / n_launched / n_surviving).

Axes ran over all 128,512 features regardless of whether describe succeeded for each. So:

    2,568 features x 5 axes = 12,840 axis rows = 2.00% of 642,410

were produced on an EVIDENCE-ONLY prompt — a second, weaker instrument silently mixed into the label set with nothing marking the boundary. This is not merely a coverage gap in `descriptions.jsonl`; it is a quality gap in the labels themselves.

It IS reconstructible downstream — left-join `axis_labels` against `descriptions` on `feat_id`, and absence means DESC was omitted — but no consumer would think to perform that join unless told. #1773's v44 caveat now states it and carries the recipe.

## 3. RE-SCOPED COST — ~$190, not ~$15

The original ~$15 was describe-only. Full recovery must also re-judge the dependent axis rows, because those 2,568 features were labelled without the description that recovery would supply:

    describe re-judge   2,602 items                              ~ $15
    axes re-judge       2,568 x 5 axes x 5 draws = 64,200 calls   ~ $175
    TOTAL                                                          ~ $190

(Realized #1773 basis: 997.4 input / 163.8 output tokens per axes call, Batch API.) Both legs require a FRESH cache dir — the rubric-keyed judge cache excludes `max_tokens` and would re-serve the failed entries (`.claude/rules/llm-judging.md` rules 22/24).

Still trivial against the run's $9,505. It buys real-feature description coverage 97.98% -> ~99.9% AND removes the mixed-instrument stratum from the axis labels, which is the part that matters for anyone using the labels as a search index.

BOUND ON RECOVERY, unchanged: 17.1% of the describe failures are EMPTY responses — a content-class outcome no parser change fixes — so recovery cannot reach 100%.

## 4. EXACT COVERAGE NUMBERS for the planner

Real features described 125,915 / 128,512 = 97.98% (2,597 missing); plus 195/200 random-direction controls = 126,110 description rows total. Axis labels 128,482 / 128,512 per axis = 99.98%.

Diagnostic lead from the #1345 judge-leg wiring round (boundary-impl, 2026-07-31): parse_judge_json's fence fallback anchors on the FIRST '{' via raw_decode — so a reason-then-score rubric that emits prose BEFORE the JSON object is exposed to a wrong-brace anchor whenever the prose contains a stray '{' (the reply then drops as unparseable). If this task's measured 2.02% fence-drops concentrate in rubrics that put reasoning OUTSIDE the JSON object, that mechanism — not fences per se — may be the dominant cause; rubrics that put reasoning INSIDE the object (reasoning key first, score key last) are structurally immune. Worth splitting the drop census by rubric shape before designing the fix.
